newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico media mogul mourned by friend and foe.
newsitem.headline: Mexico media mogul mourned by friend and foe.

text.p: Powerful friends and bitter foes on Thursday mourned the death of Emilio Azcarraga Milmo, Mexico's controversial media mogul who built his company Televisa into the world's top Spanish-langauge television empire.
The 66-year-old billionaire, who never finished high school but had the ear of every Mexican president, ran Televisa for a quarter of a century.

He succumbed to cancer in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday ending his life as he lived it -- in private opulence. The last weeks of his life were spent sailing aboard his 240-foot luxury yacht off Florida, Televisa sources said.

In its nightly news program, Televisa said a mass would be held for him in Mexico City's Basilica of Guadalupe, the country's most important shrine, at 6 p.m. (2300 GMT) Friday. It was bound to produce a phalanx of Mexico's most powerful figures.
It was not clear, however, when his ashes were due to be returned to Mexico after his cremation in Miami.

"He was an extraordinary man who provoked storms but also loyalties and friendships," Mexico's Nobel prize-winning author Octavio Paz said. "He was a fighter in the domain of modern communication, and died like a fighter."
Azcarraga was one of Mexico's most controversial figures, mainly because of his unabashed support for the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled the country for 68 years.
"The company (Televisa) is with Mexico, with the President of the Republic and is with the PRI ... we are (part) of the system," Azcarraga said in March 1990.
Televisa itself was created in 1930, just one year after the PRI was founded, and Azcarraga Milmo inherited the already important company from his father Emilio Azcarraga Vidaurreta.

He built a huge empire spanning satellites, programming, magazines, radio and network television. The group includes interests in the Spanish-language Univision network in the United States, the SKY direct-to-home satellite television project as well as in records, films and theatre.
It has also become one of the world's largest producers of soap operas, translated into dozens of languages from Polish to Portuguese.
Televisa now passes into the hands of third-generation heir Emilio Azcarraga Jean, 29.

Azcarraga Milmo, who stepped down as chairman of Televisa in March when doctors told him he had only weeks to live, was a hard-nosed businessman and one of the richest men in Latin America, worth some $2 billion last year, according to Forbes Magazine.

"In his field, he was one of the great businessmen on the world stage. One must recognize that merit," Carlos Slim, the chairman of the country's telephone giant Telefonos de Mexico Telmex (Telmex) said.

Critics complained that Televisa's news programs were slanted to help the PRI win elections and to trash the opposition. Azcarraga was also attacked for never addressing the nation's dire problems, preferring programming that showed Mexico through rose-tinted lenses.

During a fund-raising banquet by former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari ahead of the 1994 presidential election, Azcarraga was reported to have offered $50 million to help the PRI's re-election efforts -- twice what Salinas requested -- because his company had done so well from the government.

Despite the criticism, even foes lined up on Thursday to pay respects to the man known as "The Tiger." The nickname came partly from his sharp instinct for a good business deal and partly because of a hallmark stripe of white hair.
"The death of a visionary Mexican is a sad piece of news," Joaquin Vargas Guajardo, the chairman of MVS Multivision, a rival satellite and cable TV broadcaster.
